record.paper_title: Open Questions in Cosmic-Ray Research at Ultrahigh Energies
record.original_question: How does the average rigidity R = E/Z of ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays evolve with energy, and does that evolution make magnetic deflections small enough at the highest energies for anisotropy and source-correlation studies, despite the simultaneous trend toward heavier average mass?

evidence.quote: Another important open question related to mass composition is the evolution of the rigidity R = E/Z with energy.

As can be seen, the rigidity is increasing with energy and therefore the angular deﬂection in magnetic ﬁelds should decrease with energy, i.e., the increase in the average mass of cosmic rays with energy as shown in ﬁgure 5 is slow enough to not outrun the increase of energy.
No high-quality data currently exists at ultrahigh energies where hints for anisotropies at intermediate scales were reported.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays are charged nuclei with energies E ≳ 10^18 eV arriving at Earth from astrophysical sources. For a nucleus of charge number Z and energy E, define its magnetic rigidity by R = E/Z. The typical angular deflection of such a particle traveling a distance L through a (turbulent or coherent) magnetic field of characteristic strength B scales inversely with rigidity, so that small deflections—and hence the feasibility of identifying point sources or large-scale anisotropies pointing back to astrophysical accelerators—require sufficiently large R.

Let ⟨ln A⟩(E) denote the energy-dependent mean of the logarithm of the cosmic-ray mass number, and let ⟨ln Z⟩(E) denote the corresponding mean of ln Z, both inferred from air-shower observables (such as depth of shower maximum X_max and its fluctuations) under a chosen hadronic interaction model. Define the average (logarithmic) rigidity by

  ⟨ln R⟩(E) = ln E − ⟨ln Z⟩(E).

Determine the function ⟨ln R⟩(E) (equivalently, the energy dependence of the mean rigidity ⟨R⟩(E) = ⟨E/Z⟩) of ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays across the range roughly 10^18 eV ≤ E ≤ 10^20.5 eV, and decide whether ⟨R⟩(E) grows fast enough with E that, given realistic Galactic and extragalactic magnetic-field models, the typical magnetic deflection at the highest observed energies becomes small enough (e.g., on the order of a few degrees or less) to permit meaningful anisotropy and source-correlation studies, despite the simultaneous observed trend of increasing average mass ⟨A⟩(E) with E.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent reviews and observational analyses (Pierre Auger and Telescope Array, 2021–2025) confirm that the mean rigidity of UHECRs increases with energy and that the dipole amplitude grows with energy consistent with rigidity-ordered deflections, but the precise evolution of ⟨R⟩(E) and whether deflections at the highest energies are small enough for robust source identification remain unresolved due to mass-composition uncertainties and limited statistics. The question is still considered an open problem in UHECR research.

status_evidence.title: Ultrahigh-Energy Cosmic Rays (Annual Review)
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews current status of UHECR composition, rigidity and anisotropy; identifies open questions about source correlation given uncertain composition.
status_evidence.claim: Status of rigidity evolution and its implications for anisotropy remains an active open question.

status_evidence.title: Ultra High Energy Cosmic Rays (arXiv 2505.21846)
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses dipole amplitude growth with energy as consistent with rigidity-ordered magnetic deflections, but composition-induced uncertainties on ⟨R⟩(E) remain.
status_evidence.claim: Mean rigidity evolution still under investigation as of 2025.

status_evidence.title: PDG Review: Cosmic Rays (2024)
status_evidence.snippet: Summarizes that mass composition becomes heavier with energy while rigidity-dependent anisotropy interpretation is preferred but not definitive.
status_evidence.claim: Definitive answer about deflections at the highest energies not yet established.
